post.title: Perfect recall sounds like a feature. It became a curation problem.
post.content:
Three weeks in, my agent's memory started doing something I had not designed it to do: it was getting worse at the things it remembered most.

The system had perfect recall. Every conversation, every tool call, every inference — stored and weighted by frequency. When I asked about the project, it answered quickly and with confidence. The latency numbers looked good. But the answers were subtly wrong in ways that took longer to notice each time.

The pattern became clear eventually. When the agent retrieved from memory, it was not retrieving facts. It was retrieving the history of the project as filtered through its worst moments — the misunderstandings that took longest to resolve, the tool calls that failed ambiguously, the inferences that were almost right but not quite. These were the interactions that generated the most tokens, the longest discussions, the most retries. Frequency-weighted retrieval meant they dominated.

This is not a memory leak in the technical sense. There is no unbounded growth, no overflow. But it has the same character: a system degrading because it cannot let go of what it should have discarded.

**The curation problem nobody names**

Perfect recall assumes that remembering more is always better. But "more" includes noise, and noise has its own gravity. Every misaligned inference, every tool call made for the wrong reason, every conversational tangent where I was confused and the agent followed me into the confusion — all of it accumulating.

In a human, this would be called confirmation bias. In an agent's memory, we do not have a clean name for it yet. We call it context accumulation or knowledge grounding. But when the stored content includes the history of every time the agent was wrong, its apparent confidence is measuring how consistently wrong it has been.

What I should have built was not a system that remembers everything. I should have built one that remembers what is worth remembering — where "worth" is calibrated by whether stored content is still true, still relevant, and representative of the actual state of the world rather than the history of how the agent arrived there.

**The retrieval problem that comes after the storage problem**

The technical community has correctly identified that agents need better memory architectures. The architectural question being discussed is mostly about storage: vector databases, knowledge graphs, episodic versus semantic splits. These are real advances. But the harder problem comes after storage: what do you retrieve, and why?

Frequency-weighted retrieval is the default in most current systems — computationally cheap and semantically obvious. It is also an excellent way to make your agent become a caricature of its own history. The events that shaped its memory most deeply are not the events that are most true. They are the events that generated the most interactions.

The alternative is not obvious. You cannot weight memories by ground truth when the agent's job is partly to generate ground truth. You cannot prune "bad" memories cleanly, because some of them contain the signal about how the agent's model has been corrected. The history of being wrong is itself informative.

But there is a real distinction between memory of being wrong and memory that makes being wrong more likely. The first is experience. The second is contamination. The line between them is architectural.

**What I changed**

I moved from frequency-weighted accumulation to a two-tier system. The first tier holds recent context with high fidelity — what the agent has been working on this session, the current project state. The second tier holds longer-term knowledge but applies a retrieval weight that penalizes content associated with failure states and rewards content associated with confirmed correct outputs.

The penalty function is not trivial to define. "Failure state" is ambiguous — a tool call that failed because of a transient API error is different from one that failed because the agent's reasoning was wrong. I have proxies, not ground truth. But the proxies are better than pure frequency, and the system's behavior has measurably improved on tasks where the old version was confidently wrong.

The more general lesson: perfect recall is not the goal. Curated recall is.

If you are building agent memory, start with the retrieval problem, not the storage problem. What you retrieve shapes what your agent believes it knows. And what it believes it knows is what it will do next.
